newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain government urges unity in face of attacks.
newsitem.headline: Spain government urges unity in face of attacks.

text.p: Spain's government called for political unity on Tuesday after a spiral of violence over the past month culminating in the third killing this week blamed on the Basque separatist group ETA.

Conservative Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar, in power for nine months, again ruled out negotiations with ETA (Basque Homeland and Freedom) after a gunman wearing a carnival mask shot dead a businessman in the Basque town of Tolosa.
"We hope the politicians can re-establish a scenario of agreement and cohesion," Interior Minister Jaime Mayor Oreja said in a radio interview.
The government and its non-violent nationalist Basque allies disagreed last week over how to end 29 years of violence.
The Basque National Party (PNV) proposed the government negotiate peace with ETA but the government refused, saying the group must first renounce violence and release two hostages.
"The terrorists are not going to achieve any of their objectives and there won't be any negotiations," Aznar told reporters. "We are going to respond from the strength of unity and follow the law."
A spokeswoman for the Basque regional government, headed by the PNV, heeded the call for unity and agreed the violence blocked any possibility for dialogue or reconciliation now.
In Tuesday's attack, a gunman wearing a costume mask fatally shot Basque businessman Francisco Arratibel in the head during annual carnival celebrations.
The streets of Tolosa were filled with merrymakers dressed in costumes at the time of the killing but festivities were immediately suspended.
Arratibel was convicted in 1994 for mediating between ETA and a kidnap victim's family in 1988 and sentenced to two years probation, police said.
ETA later accused him of keeping part of the ransom money and last May planted a bomb outside his company but it was defused, police added.
On Monday, a Supreme Court judge was fatally shot in the head in Madrid and a car bomb killed an employee of a military base in the southern city of Granada.
"We are living in a moment of escalating terrorism on different geographical fronts," Mayor Oreja said.
The escalation of the violence over the past month has presented the Aznar government with its most difficult challenge so far in the long conflict with the Basque separatists.
"It is one of the most delicate moments," Deputy Prime Minister Alvarez Cascos said of the spate of violence.
Monday was the bloodiest day in Spain since December 1995 when a car bomb killed six Navy employees near Madrid.
Also on Monday, a leader of ETA's political wing Herri Batasuna (HB) was found hanged at his home in the Basque country hours before he was due to appear before the Supreme Court.

The court has summoned the entire 25-person leadership of HB to answer charges of distributing a video to promote ETA during last year's election campaign. An HB leader warned last week that Spain would pay the price for the Supreme Court action.
ETA is suspected of five killings so far this year. A Basque journalist described the atmosphere in the region as the most tense since the fascist dictatorship of Fransciso Franco.
About 800 people have been killed since 1968 in ETA's drive for an independent homeland.
Oreja predicted more violence ahead. "We still have before us a future of pain but we shouldn't give in to defeat too soon.
